```{r setup}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center", dpi = 300, out.width = "100%")
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(here); library(brms); library(posterior); library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr); library(knitr)
})
source(here("paper", "barg", "barg_data.R"))
source(here("paper", "barg", "barg_priors.R"))
source(here("paper", "barg", "barg_quantities.R"))

FITDIR <- here("paper", "barg", if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("BARG_QUICK"))) "fits_quick" else "fits")
gf  <- function(n) readRDS(file.path(FITDIR, paste0(n, ".rds")))
FIG <- function(n) here("paper", "barg", "figures", n)

fit_ref    <- gf("ref")
fit_prior  <- gf("prior_ref")
fit_noland <- gf("noland")
mf <- readRDS(file.path(FITDIR, "manifest.rds"))

# ---- everything the text and the tables quote ---------------------------
cf       <- coef_table(fit_ref)
icc_ref  <- icc_table(fit_ref)
icc_nol  <- icc_table(fit_noland)
cor_tb   <- cor_table(fit_ref)
ppsd_ref <- prior_post_sd(fit_ref, fit_prior)
ppc_stat_tbl <- readRDS(file.path(FITDIR, "ppc_stat_tbl.rds"))

# The six sensitivity fits are large.  They are loaded one at a time, reduced
# to the quantities the report needs, and dropped again, so that the render
# never holds more than two fits in memory at once.
SENS <- c(REF = "ref", S1 = "s1", S2 = "s2", S3 = "s3", S4 = "s4", S5 = "s5")
ppsd_s1  <- NULL
sens_long <- bind_rows(lapply(names(SENS), function(nm) {
  if (nm == "REF") {
    d <- as_draws_df(fit_ref)
  } else {
    f <- gf(SENS[[nm]])
    if (nm == "S1")
      ppsd_s1 <<- prior_post_sd(f, NULL, b_sd = setNames(rep(1, 7), resps))
    d <- as_draws_df(f); rm(f); gc()
  }
  out <- bind_rows(
    bind_rows(lapply(resps, function(r) {
      x <- icc_draws(d, r, resp_fam[[r]]); q <- eti(x)
      data.frame(Spec = nm, Quantity = paste0("ICC: ", unname(resp_lab[r])),
                 Median = median(x), lo = q[1], hi = q[2],
                 inrope = mean(x <= ICC_ROPE))
    })),
    bind_rows(lapply(resps, function(r) bind_rows(lapply(preds, function(pp) {
      x <- d[[paste0("b_", r, "_", pp)]] / link_sd[[r]]; q <- eti(x)
      data.frame(Spec = nm,
                 Quantity = paste0(unname(resp_lab[r]), " ~ ", unname(pred_lab[pp])),
                 Median = median(x), lo = q[1], hi = q[2],
                 inrope = mean(abs(x) < ROPE_SD))
    })))))
  rm(d); gc(); out
}))

dr_ref <- as_draws_df(fit_ref)
sm_ref <- summarise_draws(dr_ref, "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")
sm_ref <- sm_ref[!is.na(sm_ref$rhat) & !startsWith(sm_ref$variable, "lp"), ]
np_ref <- nuts_params(fit_ref)
n_div  <- sum(np_ref$Value[np_ref$Parameter == "divergent__"])
n_tree <- sum(np_ref$Value[np_ref$Parameter == "treedepth__"] >= 10)

fmt  <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
ci   <- function(m, l, h, d = 3) sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", fmt(m, d), fmt(l, d), fmt(h, d))
kt   <- function(x, caption, digits = 3, ...)
  knitr::kable(x, caption = caption, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE, ...)
rlab <- function(x) unname(resp_lab[x])
plab <- function(x) unname(pred_lab[x])
```

# Preamble

## Why the analysis is Bayesian {#sec-why-bayes}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Preamble A.
:::

Four considerations, none of which is a matter of taste.

**One model, four distributional families.** The seven measures on a Quina
scraper are not on one scale. Thickness and overall size are positive and
right-skewed; the geometric index of unifacial reduction (GIUR) and the
retouched share of the perimeter are proportions with mass piled at one; the
scar count is a count; the edge angle and the number of retouch generations
are treated as unbounded. A single multivariate model that gives each measure
the likelihood its scale calls for, and still shares one locality-level
random structure across all seven, is straightforward to write down and fit
by MCMC and awkward to fit any other way.

**Intervals for derived quantities.** The quantity that answers the first
research question is the share of link-scale variance attributable to
locality --- an intraclass correlation built from a variance component and a
residual variance that are themselves functions of several parameters. Under
MCMC it is computed draw by draw and inherits a genuine interval; there is no
approximation and no delta-method step.

**Support for a null value, not merely failure to reject one.** The
substantive claim under test is that the landscape variables do *not* explain
the between-locality differences. A frequentist test can only fail to reject
that; a posterior distribution combined with a region of practical
equivalence can accept it, reject it, or say that the data do not decide
(@sec-decisions).

**Intervals that do not lean on large-$N$ asymptotics.** The design has
$n = `r n_spec`$ specimens but only $`r n_loc`$ localities, and every
predictor is a locality-level attribute (@sec-data). Asymptotic intervals for
the variance component of a `r n_loc`-cluster design are not to be trusted;
posterior intervals require no such argument.

## Goals of the analysis {#sec-goals}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Preamble B.
:::

The goals are **estimation** (the magnitude of each landscape effect and of
the locality-level variance, with uncertainty) and **decision about null
values** (whether each landscape effect is small enough to be treated as
absent). Prediction of new specimens is not a goal. Formal model selection is
not a goal either: the candidate structures here are not competing scientific
hypotheses but one model whose coefficients are being estimated.

::: {.na}
**Not applicable.** Because no model comparison is performed, every BARG item
concerning Bayes factors and posterior model probabilities is inapplicable:
**3.C** (report BF and model probabilities), **4.D** (BF decision thresholds)
and **5.D** (sensitivity of the BF to the prior). No bridge sampling, no
marginal likelihood and no BF appears anywhere in this document. The
reference BARG example marks the same boundary: where the goal is estimation
rather than model comparison, the analysis is complete once the posterior and
its sensitivity have been reported.
:::

## The two research questions

**Q1. Is there technological variation between localities at all?**
Answered by the locality variance component and the intraclass correlation it
implies (@sec-icc, @sec-q1).

**Q2. Can that variation be explained by basin, elevation above the channel,
or distance to the channel?** Answered by the population-level slopes
(@sec-posterior-summary, @sec-q2).

The order is not cosmetic. If there is nothing to explain, the second
question has no content; and if the answer to Q1 is "yes" while the answer to
Q2 is "the data do not say", those are two different results and must not be
merged into one.

---

# The model {#sec-model}

## Data variables {#sec-data}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 1.A.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-data-vars
kt(data.frame(
  Variable = c(rlab(resps), "Basin", "Height above channel", "Distance to channel",
               "Locality"),
  Role = c(rep("response", 7), rep("predictor (locality level)", 3), "grouping factor"),
  Type = c("continuous, positive (mm)",
           "continuous, positive (mm); geometric mean of length, width and thickness",
           "proportion in [0, 1]", "proportion in [0, 1]", "count",
           "continuous (degrees)", "continuous (generations)",
           "binary: Binchuan / Huangping", "continuous (m)", "continuous (m)",
           "factor, 26 levels"),
  Observed = c(
    sprintf("%.1f - %.1f", sapply(resps, function(r) min(mod_dat[[r]])),
                            sapply(resps, function(r) max(mod_dat[[r]]))),
    sprintf("%d / %d", sum(mod_dat$Basin == "Binchuan"), sum(mod_dat$Basin == "Huangping")),
    sprintf("%.0f - %.0f", min(mod_dat$Height), max(mod_dat$Height)),
    sprintf("%.0f - %.0f", min(mod_dat$Distance), max(mod_dat$Distance)),
    sprintf("%d specimens in %d localities", n_spec, n_loc))),
  caption = "The variables entering the model, and their observed range in the analysed sample.")
```

**How size is defined.** `GMsize` is the geometric mean of the three linear
dimensions,
$$\mathrm{GMsize} = (\mathrm{Length}\times\mathrm{Width}\times\mathrm{Thickness})^{1/3},$$
computed for each specimen. This definition lives only in the code of the
original analysis; it is stated here because it has a consequence.

**GMsize and Thickness are related by construction.** Thickness is one of the
three factors in GMsize, so the two responses share a component before any
archaeology enters. The model is fitted with `set_rescor(FALSE)`, which
assumes the *residuals* of the seven responses are independent given the
locality intercepts. That assumption is not credible for this pair. The
practical consequence is confined: the slopes and their intervals for each
response are still valid marginally, because with `rescor = FALSE` the
multivariate model factorises into seven univariate models sharing only the
correlated random intercepts; what is not valid is any statement about the
*joint* uncertainty of, say, the thickness slope and the size slope, and any
reading of the two as independent evidence. The observed correlation between
the locality intercepts of the two (@sec-cor) should therefore be read as
partly mechanical.

**Which specimens are analysed.**

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dropped
kt(drop_log |> mutate(lost = c(NA, diff(n))) |>
     rename(`specimens remaining` = n, `lost at this step` = lost),
   caption = "Complete-case filtering. One specimen was dropped, for a missing GIUR.",
   digits = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-localities
kt(mod_dat |> count(Basin, Locality) |> count(Basin, name = "localities") |>
     left_join(mod_dat |> count(Basin, name = "specimens"), by = "Basin") |>
     mutate(`specimens per locality` = sprintf("%d - %d",
       tapply(mod_dat$Locality, mod_dat$Basin, function(x) min(table(droplevels(x)))),
       tapply(mod_dat$Locality, mod_dat$Basin, function(x) max(table(droplevels(x)))))),
   caption = "Localities and specimens by basin. Heqing, which appears under that name in the site table, is folded into Huangping: the two names refer to the same basin.",
   digits = 0)
```

**$n = `r n_spec`$ is a specimen count, not an information count.** All three
predictors --- basin, height above the channel, distance to the channel ---
are constant within a locality. For the population-level slopes the design
therefore carries close to `r n_loc` independent units, not `r n_spec`, and
the `r n_loc` are unevenly filled: the largest locality contributes
`r max(table(mod_dat$Locality))` specimens and `r sum(table(mod_dat$Locality) == 1)`
localities contribute one each. Basin is worse still: it is a single binary
contrast between `r sum(tapply(as.character(mod_dat$Basin), mod_dat$Locality, function(x) x[1]) == "Binchuan")`
and `r sum(tapply(as.character(mod_dat$Basin), mod_dat$Locality, function(x) x[1]) == "Huangping")`
localities. The random intercept is what keeps the specimen count from being
read as `r n_spec` independent observations of the landscape effects, and the
width of the intervals in @sec-posterior-summary is the honest consequence.

**The standardisation is specimen-weighted.** `zHeight` and `zDistance` are
centred and scaled over the `r n_spec` specimens, not over the `r n_loc`
localities, so a locality enters the centring and the scaling with the weight
of its own assemblage. A locality-weighted standardisation would give
slightly different numerical slopes on a rescaled axis; it would not change
any decision, because every slope is reported divided by the link-scale SD of
its own response and the ROPE moves with it.

## Likelihood and parameters {#sec-likelihood}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 1.B.
:::

For specimen $i$ in locality $j$, each response $r$ has its own likelihood
with a linear predictor on its own link scale:

$$
g_r(\mu^{(r)}_{ij}) \;=\; \beta^{(r)}_{0} \;+\; \beta^{(r)}_{\text{Basin}}\,\mathrm{Basin}_j
\;+\; \beta^{(r)}_{\text{H}}\,\mathrm{zHeight}_j
\;+\; \beta^{(r)}_{\text{D}}\,\mathrm{zDistance}_j \;+\; u^{(r)}_j ,
$$

$$
\bigl(u^{(1)}_j,\dots,u^{(7)}_j\bigr)^{\!\top} \sim
\mathrm{MVNormal}\bigl(\mathbf 0,\;\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Omega\,\mathbf D\bigr),
\qquad \mathbf D=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma^{(1)}_u,\dots,\sigma^{(7)}_u).
$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-likelihood
kt(data.frame(
  Response = rlab(resps),
  Likelihood = unname(fam_lab[resp_fam]),
  `Link for the mean` = unname(link_lab[resp_fam]),
  `Auxiliary parameters` = c("sigma", "sigma", "phi, zoi, coi", "phi, zoi, coi",
                             "shape", "sigma", "sigma"),
  `Link-scale SD` = round(link_sd, 3), check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Likelihoods. The last column is the SD of the observed response on its own link scale; it is the unit in which every slope and every ROPE below is expressed.")
```

**Parameters of theoretical interest versus nuisance parameters.** Of the
`r nrow(sm_ref)` estimated parameters, the ones the research questions are
about are the `r nrow(cf)` population-level slopes $\beta^{(r)}_{\text{Basin}},
\beta^{(r)}_{\text{H}}, \beta^{(r)}_{\text{D}}$ (Q2) and the seven
locality SDs $\sigma^{(r)}_u$ together with the ICCs derived from them (Q1).
The seven intercepts, the auxiliary parameters (`sigma`, `phi`, `shape`,
`zoi`, `coi`) and the 21 elements of $\boldsymbol\Omega$ are needed to make
the model coherent but carry no hypothesis. The correlations are nevertheless
reported in full (@sec-cor), because they were estimated and BARG asks for
every parameter of the model to be described.

**Partial pooling.** With `r sum(table(mod_dat$Locality) == 1)` localities of
one specimen, the locality offsets are strongly shrunk towards the grand mean;
the caterpillar plot in @sec-cor shows how far. This is the intended
behaviour, and it is why the ICC is not simply a between-group variance ratio
computed from raw locality means.

::: {.na}
**A trap in the zero-one-inflated beta parameterisation.** For GIUR and the
retouched perimeter, the three predictors enter **only** the beta component's
mean `mu`. The inflation parameters `zoi` (the probability that a value is
exactly 0 or exactly 1) and `coi` (the probability that such a value is 1
rather than 0) are pure intercepts, constant across basins, elevations and
distances. Two consequences must be kept in mind when reading any GIUR or RLI
number in this report:

1. A reported slope is the effect on the **logit of the beta-component mean,
   conditional on the value lying strictly inside (0, 1)**. It is *not* the
   effect on the unconditional expected GIUR, which also moves with `zoi` and
   `coi`.
2. The ICC for these two responses is likewise computed from the beta
   component alone and ignores the inflation entirely.

In this sample there are `r sum(mod_dat$GIUR == 1)` specimens with GIUR
exactly 1 and `r sum(mod_dat$GIUR == 0)` with GIUR exactly 0, and
`r sum(mod_dat$RLI == 1)` and `r sum(mod_dat$RLI == 0)` for the retouched
perimeter. There is therefore no zero inflation at all to model: the fitted
`coi` is a posterior over "all inflated values are ones", which the data
determine almost completely, and the zero-inflation half of the family is
supported by nothing. The family is effectively a one-inflated beta.
:::

## Prior distributions and their justification {#sec-priors}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 1.C.
:::

### The problem with the original prior

The model as originally specified put `normal(0, 1)` on every
population-level slope of all seven responses and `student_t(3, 0, 2)` on
every locality SD, and left **every other class** at its brms default. Both
halves of that are defects.

**What was left unreported.** These are the priors the original fit actually
used for everything except `b` and `sd`, none of which appeared in any
write-up:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-default-priors
gp <- brms::get_prior(fit_ref$formula, data = mod_dat)
gp <- as.data.frame(gp)
gp <- gp[gp$prior != "" & !(gp$class %in% c("b", "sd")), ]
gp |>
  transmute(Class = class, Response = ifelse(resp == "", "--", rlab(resp)),
            Group = ifelse(group == "", "--", group),
            `brms default` = prior,
            Comment = case_when(
              class == "Intercept" ~ "data-dependent: centred and scaled on the observed response",
              class == "cor"       ~ "the 7 x 7 LKJ prior, never reported",
              class == "phi"       ~ "near-improper; mass arbitrarily close to zero",
              class == "shape"     ~ "very heavy right tail",
              class %in% c("zoi", "coi") ~ "uniform on (0, 1); proper, but unstated",
              TRUE                 ~ "half-t scaled on the observed response")) |>
  kt(caption = "The brms defaults the original specification inherited without reporting them. The Intercept and sigma rows are read off the data, which makes them empirical priors, not the vague priors a reader would assume.")
```

**A single prior scale across three link scales.** The seven responses reach
their linear predictor through three different links (log, logit, identity),
and their link-scale SDs span two orders of magnitude, from
`r fmt(min(link_sd), 3)` for `r rlab(names(which.min(link_sd)))` to
`r fmt(max(link_sd), 2)` for `r rlab(names(which.max(link_sd)))`
(@tbl-likelihood). A `normal(0, 1)` slope prior is therefore a very different
statement about each. The clearest way to see it is the share of the prior
that falls inside that response's own ROPE --- the interval of slopes the
analysis is prepared to call practically zero:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior-rope
pir <- data.frame(Response = rlab(resps),
                  `Link-scale SD` = round(link_sd, 3),
                  `ROPE half-width` = round(ROPE_SD * link_sd, 4),
                  `normal(0, 1)` = round(prior_in_rope(rep(1, 7)), 2),
                  `normal(0, SD_link)` = round(prior_in_rope(link_sd), 2),
                  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
kt(pir, caption = "Percentage of the slope prior lying inside the response's own ROPE, before and after the correction. Under the original prior the same nominal specification ranged from an almost dogmatic rejection of a null effect to an almost dogmatic assertion of one; under the corrected prior it is 7.97% for every response, by construction.")
```

**Where it mattered.** The diagnostic that turns this from an aesthetic
complaint into a substantive one is the ratio of the posterior SD to the
prior SD for each slope. A ratio near 1 means the posterior is the prior and
the data contributed nothing.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppsd
ppsd_cmp <- ppsd_s1 |>
  transmute(Response, Predictor, `normal(0, 1)` = ratio) |>
  left_join(ppsd_ref |> transmute(Response, Predictor, `normal(0, SD_link)` = ratio),
            by = c("Response", "Predictor")) |>
  mutate(Response = rlab(Response), Predictor = plab(Predictor))
kt(ppsd_cmp, caption = "Posterior SD divided by prior SD, for every slope, under the original prior (S1) and under the reference prior. Values near 1 mean the data did not move the prior. The prior SD is taken from the sample_prior = 'only' draws for the reference prior and analytically for normal(0, 1).")
```

```{r}
#| label: ppsd-summary
#| echo: false
ea_old <- ppsd_cmp |> filter(Response == rlab("EdgeAngle"))
ea_new_max <- max(ea_old$`normal(0, SD_link)`)
```

Under `normal(0, 1)` the `r rlab("EdgeAngle")` slopes had posterior/prior SD
ratios of
`r paste(fmt(sort(ea_old[["normal(0, 1)"]]), 2), collapse = ", ")` --- the
posterior was very nearly the prior, and the reported edge-angle result was
mostly a restatement of an arbitrary choice. Under the corrected prior the
largest of the three is `r fmt(ea_new_max, 2)`.

### The reference prior

Every class that `get_prior()` lists is given an explicit prior; nothing is
left at a brms default. Two reasons. BARG Step 1.C asks for the prior to be
reported in full, and a brms default is not a reported prior --- in
particular the default intercept prior is `student_t(3, median(y), 2.5 mad(y))`,
which is a prior read off the data. And `sample_prior = "only"`, needed for
the prior predictive check of @sec-prior-pred, requires every prior to be
proper.

| Class | Prior | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `b` (slopes) | `normal(0, SD_link)` per response | one prior SD equal to the whole observed spread of that response on its own link scale: an effect as large as the response's total variation is a priori about one SD out. Puts `r fmt(prior_in_rope(link_sd)[1], 2)`% of the prior inside the ROPE for all seven. |
| `Intercept` | see below | fixed from the measurement scale, not from the sample |
| `sd` (locality) | `student_t(3, 0, 2)` | heavy-tailed half-$t$; carried over unchanged from the original specification and varied in S3 and S4 |
| `sigma` | `student_t(3, 0, SD_link)` | half-$t$ scaled to the response, for the same reason as `b` |
| `phi` (zoib) | `gamma(2, 0.1)` | proper, mean 20, density zero at the origin. The brms default `gamma(0.01, 0.01)` piles mass arbitrarily close to zero, where the beta density is degenerate, and makes the prior predictive distribution unusable |
| `shape` (negbin) | `gamma(2, 0.1)` | same; the brms default `inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3)` has an extremely heavy right tail |
| `zoi`, `coi` | `beta(1, 1)` | uniform on (0, 1); this is also the brms default, stated here rather than inherited |
| `cor` (7x7) | `lkj(1)` | uniform over correlation matrices; varied in S5 |

**Intercept priors.** These are set from what a lithic analyst would have
called possible for a retouched flake tool before seeing these
`r n_spec` pieces, mapped through the link. Each is far wider than the
observed spread.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-intercept-prior
kt(data.frame(
  Response = rlab(resps), Link = unname(link_lab[resp_fam]),
  Prior = unname(intercept_prior[resps]),
  `Implied 95% range on the response scale` = c(
    "6 - 100 mm", "12 - 134 mm", "GIUR 0.05 - 0.95", "0.05 - 0.95 of the perimeter",
    "3 - 143 scars", "26 - 104 degrees", "-0.9 - 6.9 generations"),
  `Observed mean` = c(sprintf("%.1f mm", mean(mod_dat$Thickness)),
                      sprintf("%.1f mm", mean(mod_dat$GMsize)),
                      sprintf("%.2f", mean(mod_dat$GIUR)),
                      sprintf("%.2f", mean(mod_dat$RLI)),
                      sprintf("%.0f", mean(mod_dat$NScar)),
                      sprintf("%.1f deg", mean(mod_dat$EdgeAngle)),
                      sprintf("%.2f", mean(mod_dat$RG))),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Intercept priors, fixed from the measurement scale rather than from the sample.")
```

**One honest qualification.** The scale of the slope prior and of the `sigma`
prior is taken from the link-scale SD of the response, which is a function of
the data. This is a unit-setting use of the data, not a location-setting one:
it fixes what "one unit of effect" means without expressing any belief about
where the effect lies, and it is the standard construction behind weakly
informative priors. It is nonetheless a mild empirical-Bayes element and is
declared here rather than buried. S1 and S2 in @sec-sensitivity vary this
scale by factors of roughly 1/8 to 2.5 and show what turns on it.

### The prior in full

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior-summary
ps <- as.data.frame(prior_summary(fit_ref))[
  , c("prior", "class", "coef", "group", "resp", "dpar", "lb", "ub", "source")]
n_inherit <- sum(ps$prior == "")
n_flat    <- sum(ps$prior == "" & ps$coef == "")
ps |>
  filter(prior != "") |>
  arrange(class, resp) |>
  select(-source) |>
  kt(caption = "prior_summary(fit_ref), every non-empty row.")
```

`r n_inherit` further rows have an empty `prior` field. Every one of them
names a specific `coef` and inherits the prior of its class; they are omitted
above. **Rows that specify no `coef` and are still empty --- that is, genuinely
flat priors: `r n_flat`.** That is the condition `sample_prior = "only"`
imposes, and it is why the prior predictive draws of @sec-prior-pred exist at
all: with a flat prior anywhere, brms cannot sample from the prior. The prior
predictive fit ran, so the condition holds.

```{r}
#| label: prior-source
#| echo: false
n_user <- sum(ps$prior != "" & ps$source == "user")
n_def  <- sum(ps$prior != "" & ps$source != "user")
def_rows <- ps |> filter(prior != "", source != "user") |>
  transmute(class, resp, group, prior)
```

**A word on the `source` column.** `r n_user` of the
`r n_user + n_def` non-empty rows are marked `user`. The remaining
`r n_def` are marked `default`, and it would be wrong to leave that
unexplained:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior-default-rows
kt(def_rows, caption = "The rows prior_summary() still labels 'default'.")
```

They are not priors the sampler uses. The `sd` rows carry no `group`: they sit
one level above the `sd` + `Locality` rows that were set explicitly, and brms
takes the most specific match, so these parents are never reached. The `L` row
is brms's own restatement of the user-supplied `lkj(1)` in the Cholesky
parameterisation it actually samples in.

The authoritative record is not `prior_summary()` but the generated Stan
program (@sec-formal). Its prior block, extracted verbatim, is the complete
list of what was added to the log posterior:

```{r}
#| label: stan-lprior
lines <- strsplit(brms::stancode(fit_ref), "\n")[[1]]
lp    <- grep("lprior \\+=", lines)
last  <- max(lp)
while (grepl("^\\s*-", lines[last + 1])) last <- last + 1   # continuation lines
cat(paste(trimws(lines[min(lp):last]), collapse = "\n"))
```

## Formal specification {#sec-formal}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 1.D.
:::

```{r}
#| label: brms-formula
fit_ref$formula
```

The Stan program brms generated from it, in full:

```{r}
#| label: stan-code
#| attr-output: "style='max-height:420px;overflow:auto;'"
cat(brms::stancode(fit_ref))
```

## Prior predictive check {#sec-prior-pred}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 1.E.
:::

The reference prior was refitted with `sample_prior = "only"`, so the draws
below come from the prior alone with the data unseen. The question is not
whether the simulated data look like the observed data --- they should not,
or the prior would be doing the data's work --- but whether they are
**physically possible**: no negative thicknesses, edge angles inside the range
a goniometer can return, GIUR inside its definitional bounds, scar counts
that a flake could carry.

```{r}
#| label: fig-prior-pred
#| fig-cap: "Prior predictive distributions (grey) against the observed distribution (dark), one panel per response. Axes are clipped to the physically possible range of each measure; the table below reports what falls outside."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("ppc_prior.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior-pred
ppd <- brms::posterior_predict(fit_prior, ndraws = 400)
bound <- list(Thickness = c(0, 150), GMsize = c(0, 250), GIUR = c(0, 1), RLI = c(0, 1),
              NScar = c(0, 400), EdgeAngle = c(0, 180), RG = c(0, 12))
kt(bind_rows(lapply(resps, function(r) {
  y <- as.vector(if (is.list(ppd)) ppd[[r]] else ppd[, , r])
  b <- bound[[r]]
  data.frame(Response = rlab(r),
             `physically possible range` = sprintf("%g - %g", b[1], b[2]),
             `prior-predictive median` = median(y),
             `prior-predictive 2.5%` = unname(quantile(y, 0.025)),
             `prior-predictive 97.5%` = unname(quantile(y, 0.975)),
             `% outside the possible range` = 100 * mean(y < b[1] | y > b[2]),
             check.names = FALSE)
})), caption = "Prior predictive draws against the physically possible range of each measure. GIUR and the retouched perimeter cannot leave [0, 1] under the zero-one-inflated beta, so their zero is structural.", digits = 2)
```

The prior predictive distributions are wide --- deliberately, since they
encode ignorance about the effects --- but they stay inside the possible
range of every measure. The prior passes.

## Chain convergence {#sec-convergence}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 2.B.
:::

For the reference fit: divergent transitions **`r n_div`**, iterations at
maximum treedepth **`r n_tree`**, largest $\hat R$ over all
`r nrow(sm_ref)` estimated parameters **`r fmt(max(sm_ref$rhat), 4)`**.

Because every conclusion in this report leans on more than the reference fit
--- the intercept-only model carries the Q1 comparison and the five prior
variants carry the sensitivity analysis --- the same diagnostics are given for
all nine runs:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diag-all
mf$diagnostics |>
  transmute(Fit = fit, `parameters` = n_par, `max Rhat` = max_rhat,
            `min bulk ESS` = round(min_ess_bulk),
            `min tail ESS` = round(min_ess_tail),
            `divergent transitions` = divergent,
            `at max treedepth` = max_treedepth) |>
  kt(caption = sprintf("Diagnostics for all nine runs, each of %s post-warmup draws.",
                       format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ",")), digits = 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: div-readout
#| echo: false
d_any <- mf$diagnostics |> filter(divergent > 0)
```

`r if (nrow(d_any) == 0) "No run produced a divergent transition." else sprintf("%d of the nine runs produced a small number of divergent transitions -- %s -- against %s draws each, that is at most %s%% of the transitions in any run. Divergences at this rate in a hierarchical model with 26 clusters and a 7 x 7 correlation matrix indicate mild curvature in the posterior near zero variance rather than a failure to explore it; the affected runs' Rhat and ESS are indistinguishable from the clean ones, and their posteriors coincide with the reference in @fig-sens-icc. They are reported rather than removed.", nrow(d_any), paste(sprintf("%s: %d", d_any$fit, d_any$divergent), collapse = ", "), format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ","), fmt(100 * max(d_any$divergent) / mf$ndraws, 3))`

```{r}

#| fig-cap: "Rhat (A) and bulk effective sample size (B) for every estimated parameter, and for the seven ICCs, which are derived quantities computed draw by draw and diagnosed like any other."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("convergence.png"))
```

## Chain resolution {#sec-resolution}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 2.C.
:::

Kruschke (2021) suggests an ESS of about 10,000, with the explicit
qualification that the figure is aimed at the stability of HDI limits and
that quantile-based limits are less demanding. This report is quantile-based
throughout (@sec-posterior-summary), so both things are given: the ESS, and
the Monte Carlo standard error of each quantile that is actually reported.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-convergence
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence and resolution for every parameter of the model and for the seven derived ICCs. Median and equal-tailed limits are given with their Monte Carlo standard errors; mode and HDI limits are given alongside, following the reference BARG document."
full_tbl <- bind_rows(
  bind_rows(lapply(sm_ref$variable, function(v) {
    x <- dr_ref[[v]]; s <- draw_summary(x)
    d <- sm_ref[sm_ref$variable == v, ]
    data.frame(Parameter = v, s, rhat = d$rhat,
               ess_bulk = d$ess_bulk, ess_tail = d$ess_tail)
  })),
  icc_ref |> transmute(Parameter = paste0("ICC_", Response), Median, CrI_lo, CrI_hi,
                       Mode, HDI_lo, HDI_hi, MCSE_lo, MCSE_med, MCSE_hi, SD,
                       rhat, ess_bulk, ess_tail))
full_tbl |>
  transmute(Parameter,
            `median` = Median, `2.5%` = CrI_lo, `97.5%` = CrI_hi,
            `mode` = Mode, `HDI lo` = HDI_lo, `HDI hi` = HDI_hi,
            `MCSE 2.5%` = MCSE_lo, `MCSE median` = MCSE_med, `MCSE 97.5%` = MCSE_hi,
            `Rhat` = rhat, `ESS bulk` = round(ess_bulk), `ESS tail` = round(ess_tail)) |>
  kt(caption = NULL, digits = 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: ess-summary
#| echo: false
min_bulk <- min(full_tbl$ess_bulk, na.rm = TRUE)
min_tail <- min(full_tbl$ess_tail, na.rm = TRUE)
worst    <- full_tbl$Parameter[which.min(full_tbl$ess_bulk)]
rel_all  <- with(full_tbl, MCSE_med / SD)
rel_all  <- rel_all[is.finite(rel_all)]
mcse_rel <- max(rel_all)
mcse_par <- full_tbl$Parameter[which.max(replace(with(full_tbl, MCSE_med / SD),
                                                 !is.finite(with(full_tbl, MCSE_med / SD)), -Inf))]
n_below_10k <- sum(full_tbl$ess_bulk < 10000, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Smallest bulk ESS: **`r format(round(min_bulk), big.mark = ",")`**
(`r worst`); smallest tail ESS:
**`r format(round(min_tail), big.mark = ",")`**.
`r n_below_10k` of the `r nrow(full_tbl)` quantities have a bulk ESS below
Kruschke's 10,000, so the recommendation is not met everywhere even at
`r format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ",")` draws. What matters for a
quantile-based report is the Monte Carlo error of the quantiles themselves.
The largest MCSE of a reported median, as a fraction of that parameter's own
posterior SD, is **`r fmt(mcse_rel, 4)`** (`r mcse_par`) --- the simulation
noise in the numbers this report quotes is about
**`r format(round(1 / mcse_rel), big.mark = ",")` times smaller** than the
posterior uncertainty it describes, and the full per-parameter MCSEs are in
@tbl-convergence for anyone who wants to check a particular one.

## Items not applicable {#sec-2d}

::: {.na}
**BARG 2.D** concerns the accuracy of approximations used in place of exact
posterior sampling --- variational inference, Laplace approximation, INLA and
the like. No approximation of that kind is used here: every posterior in this
document is a full MCMC sample from the exact posterior. The item is
inapplicable.
:::

### The checks that were specified in advance {#sec-ppc-stats}

```{r}
#| label: fig-ppc-stats
#| fig-cap: "Targeted posterior predictive statistics. Diamond: the observed value. Open circle and bar: the median and 95% interval of the same statistic over the replicated datasets. Green means the observation falls inside the interval."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("ppc_stats.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppc-stats
ppc_stat_tbl |>
  mutate(Response = rlab(Response),
         inside = observed >= rep_lo & observed <= rep_hi,
         verdict = ifelse(inside, "reproduced", "NOT reproduced")) |>
  transmute(Response, Statistic, observed,
            `replicated median` = rep_median, `2.5%` = rep_lo, `97.5%` = rep_hi,
            verdict) |>
  kt(caption = "Observed test statistics against their posterior predictive distributions.")
```

```{r}
#| label: ppc-readout
#| echo: false
gs <- function(r, s) ppc_stat_tbl[ppc_stat_tbl$Response == r & ppc_stat_tbl$Statistic == s, ]
rg_neg <- gs("RG", "share below zero"); rg_min <- gs("RG", "minimum")
gi_one <- gs("GIUR", "share exactly 1"); rl_one <- gs("RLI", "share exactly 1")
ns_disp <- gs("NScar", "variance / mean")
```

**Does the gaussian likelihood for retouch generations predict negative
values?** The observed share of retouch-generation values below zero is
`r fmt(rg_neg$observed, 3)`; over the replicated datasets the share has median
`r fmt(rg_neg$rep_median, 3)` and 95% interval
[`r fmt(rg_neg$rep_lo, 3)`, `r fmt(rg_neg$rep_hi, 3)`]. The observed minimum
is `r fmt(rg_min$observed, 2)` against a replicated interval of
[`r fmt(rg_min$rep_lo, 2)`, `r fmt(rg_min$rep_hi, 2)`]. The gaussian's
support extends below zero, but the fitted mean sits far enough above it
relative to the residual SD that impossible values are not in practice
generated. What the gaussian does miss is the *discreteness*: retouch
generations are recorded as a small number of counted generations averaged
over at most three edges, so the observed distribution is a spike train and
the replicated one is smooth. That is visible in @fig-post-pred and is a real
limitation, though not one that biases a location parameter.

Because the check is a judgement call rather than a pass/fail, a lognormal
refit of the same response is provided as a comparison, so a reader can see
directly whether the choice of family moves the conclusions:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rg-alt
# the RG response is on the log link in the comparison fit, so its ROPE has to
# be rebuilt from the log-scale SD rather than taken from link_sd
ls_ln  <- sd(log(mod_dat$RG))
dr_ln  <- local({ f <- gf("ref_rg_ln"); d <- as_draws_df(f); rm(f); gc(); d })
rg_alt <- bind_rows(lapply(preds, function(pp) {
  x <- dr_ln[[paste0("b_RG_", pp)]] / ls_ln
  q <- eti(x); p <- 100 * mean(abs(x) < ROPE_SD)
  data.frame(Family = "lognormal (comparison)", Predictor = plab(pp),
             `standardised median` = median(x), `2.5%` = q[1], `97.5%` = q[2],
             `% in ROPE` = p,
             Verdict = rope_verdict(q[1], q[2], p, ROPE_SD),
             check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
bind_rows(
  cf |> filter(Response == "RG") |>
    transmute(Family = "gaussian (reference)", Predictor = plab(Predictor),
              `standardised median` = Std_median,
              `2.5%` = Std_lo, `97.5%` = Std_hi,
              `% in ROPE` = pct_in_ROPE, Verdict),
  rg_alt) |>
  arrange(Predictor, Family) |>
  kt(caption = "Retouch generations: the reference gaussian fit against a lognormal refit of the same response. Both are shown on their own standardised axis, so the ROPE is +/- 0.1 in each case.")
```

**Do the zero-one-inflated beta fits reproduce the pile-up at 1?** For GIUR
the observed share of exact ones is `r fmt(gi_one$observed, 3)` against a
replicated interval of [`r fmt(gi_one$rep_lo, 3)`, `r fmt(gi_one$rep_hi, 3)`];
for the retouched perimeter, `r fmt(rl_one$observed, 3)` against
[`r fmt(rl_one$rep_lo, 3)`, `r fmt(rl_one$rep_hi, 3)`]. The share of exact
zeros is 0 in the data and 0 in the replications, which is not evidence that
the model captures zero inflation --- it is evidence that the zero-inflation
half of the family is estimating a probability the data have pinned at
essentially zero. See the note in @sec-likelihood.

**Is the overdispersion of the scar count captured?** The observed
variance-to-mean ratio is `r fmt(ns_disp$observed, 2)`, well above the value
of 1 a Poisson would imply; the replicated interval is
[`r fmt(ns_disp$rep_lo, 2)`, `r fmt(ns_disp$rep_hi, 2)`]. The negative
binomial captures it.

## Posterior summary {#sec-posterior-summary}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 3.B.
:::

::: {.barg}
**Declaration of interval type.** Every interval in this report is a **95%
equal-tailed (percentile) credible interval**, running from the 2.5th to the
97.5th posterior percentile, and every point summary in the text is the
**posterior median**. This is the quantile-based convention, not the
density-based one. The density-based pair --- posterior **mode** and 95%
**highest-density interval** --- is reported alongside in @tbl-convergence and
@tbl-coef-full, following the reference BARG document, so that a reader who
prefers it is not obliged to recompute anything.

## Locality-level variance and correlation structure {#sec-icc}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 3.B, for the parameters that answer Q1.
:::

The intraclass correlation is
$\mathrm{ICC}^{(r)} = \sigma_u^{(r)2} / (\sigma_u^{(r)2} + \sigma_{\text{resid}}^{(r)2})$,
computed **draw by draw** so that it carries a full posterior. The residual
variance is taken on the link scale, and its form depends on the family:
$\sigma^2$ for the gaussian and lognormal responses;
$\log(1 + 1/\mu + 1/\text{shape})$ evaluated at the intercept for the
negative binomial; and $\psi'(\mu\phi) + \psi'((1-\mu)\phi)$ --- the
logit-scale variance of the beta component --- for the two zero-one-inflated
beta responses. For those two the ICC therefore describes the beta component
only, and ignores the inflation (@sec-likelihood).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-icc
icc_ref |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response), Family = unname(fam_lab[Family]),
            `locality SD` = sd_median, `SD 2.5%` = sd_lo, `SD 97.5%` = sd_hi,
            `ICC median` = Median, `2.5%` = CrI_lo, `97.5%` = CrI_hi,
            `ICC mode` = Mode, `HDI lo` = HDI_lo, `HDI hi` = HDI_hi,
            `P(ICC > 0.05)` = P_gt_rope, Rhat = rhat,
            `ESS bulk` = round(ess_bulk), Verdict) |>
  arrange(desc(`ICC median`)) |>
  kt(caption = "Locality SD and intraclass correlation, with diagnostics for the derived quantity.", digits = 3)
```

# Decisions {#sec-decisions}

## Why decisions, and under what rule {#sec-decision-rule}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 4.A.
:::

The substantive question is not only "how large is the effect" but "is it
small enough to treat as absent". An interval alone does not answer that, and
neither does a $p$-value, which can only fail to reject. The rule used here
is Kruschke's (2018) three-way decision with a region of practical
equivalence:

| Decision | Condition (either suffices) |
|---|---|
| **Reject the null value** | the 95% credible interval lies entirely outside the ROPE, **or** less than 2.5% of the posterior mass is inside it |
| **Accept the null value** | the 95% credible interval lies entirely inside the ROPE, **or** more than 95% of the posterior mass is inside it |
| **Undecided** | neither of the above |

"Undecided" is a substantive outcome, not a failure. It means the data are
compatible both with an effect large enough to matter and with none.

## Item not applicable {#sec-4b}

::: {.na}
**BARG 4.B** asks for the loss or utility function where decisions are made
by formal decision theory. No loss function is specified here: there is no
cost structure attached to being wrong about an edge-angle slope, and
inventing one would be a fiction. The decision rule of @sec-decision-rule is
used instead, and the ROPE curve of @sec-rope makes the whole family of
decisions available rather than committing to one.
:::

## The ROPE and its justification {#sec-rope}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 4.C.
:::

The ROPE half-width used in the text is **0.1 times the SD of the response on
its own link scale** --- so a slope is "practically zero" if moving a
predictor by one unit shifts the response by less than a tenth of that
response's total spread. Expressing it in link-scale SD units is what lets
one number serve seven responses on three link scales (@tbl-prior-rope).

**Two things must be said plainly about it.**

First, the value 0.1 is a convention. It is not derived from any
archaeological argument about how large a difference in edge angle or scar
count would have to be before a lithic analyst would call it a real
difference in technological behaviour. No such argument exists in the
literature for these measures, and it would be dishonest to construct one
here.

Second --- and this is the more serious point --- BARG asks for ROPE limits
to be fixed by theoretical and practical considerations *before the results
are seen*. That precondition is not met in this analysis: the model had
already been fitted and inspected before this report was written. Choosing a
half-width now, with the posteriors in view, would let the bound be tuned
until it delivered a preferred verdict.

The response is therefore not to defend a single number but to **report the
whole curve** --- the posterior mass inside the ROPE as a continuous function
of the half-width --- and let a reader who has a defensible bound of their own
read off the answer at it. This is the same device the equivalence $p$-value
curves of the companion analysis use, for the same reason.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rope
#| fig-cap: "Posterior mass inside the ROPE as a function of the ROPE half-width, in link-scale SD units, for all 21 slopes. Dashed vertical line: the 0.1 half-width quoted in the text. Dotted horizontals: the 2.5% and 95% thresholds of the decision rule. A curve that has not reached 95% by a half-width the reader considers archaeologically negligible is a slope this design cannot declare absent."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("rope_curves.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rope-grid
#| tbl-cap: "The same information numerically: posterior mass inside the ROPE (%) at a range of half-widths, for every slope."
grid_pts <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5)
rope_curve(fit_ref, grid = grid_pts) |>
  mutate(Response = rlab(Response), Predictor = plab(Predictor),
         half = paste0("+/- ", half)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = half, values_from = pct) |>
  kt(caption = NULL, digits = 1)
```

## Item not applicable {#sec-4d}

::: {.na}
**BARG 4.D** asks for the Bayes-factor thresholds used to make decisions. No
Bayes factor is used (@sec-goals, @sec-3c). Inapplicable.
:::

## Decisions, with the estimates they rest on {#sec-verdicts}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 4.E, which requires the decision to be accompanied by the
estimate and its interval, never reported on its own.
:::

### Q1: the locality variance

```{r}
#| label: tbl-icc-decision
icc_ref |>
  arrange(desc(P_gt_rope)) |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response),
            `ICC median [95% ETI]` = ci(Median, CrI_lo, CrI_hi),
            `P(ICC > 0.05)` = fmt(P_gt_rope, 3),
            Decision = Verdict) |>
  kt(caption = "Q1 decisions. The ROPE for the ICC is [0, 0.05]: a locality share of link-scale variance below 5% is treated as negligible. Unlike the slope ROPE this bound is one-sided and has a natural reading -- 5% of variance is a share no archaeological argument would build on.")
```

### Q2: the landscape slopes

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coef-decision
cf |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response), Predictor = plab(Predictor),
            `median [95% ETI], link scale` = ci(Median, CrI_lo, CrI_hi),
            `standardised` = ci(Std_median, Std_lo, Std_hi, 2),
            `% in ROPE` = fmt(pct_in_ROPE, 1),
            `direction certainty` = fmt(Dir_certainty, 3),
            Decision = Verdict) |>
  kt(caption = "Q2 decisions at the 0.1 SD ROPE, with the estimate and interval each rests on. 'Direction certainty' is max(P(beta > 0), P(beta < 0)): 0.5 means the posterior is split evenly about zero, 1.0 that the sign is certain.")
```

### What this design could have decided: the smallest acceptable ROPE {#sec-min-rope}

An "undecided" verdict is not an empty result. For each slope there is a
smallest ROPE half-width at which the 95% interval would have fitted entirely
inside --- namely $\max(|\text{lower}|, |\text{upper}|)$. Anything wider than
that, this design *can* declare practically zero; anything narrower, it
cannot. Translating that bound into the response's own units turns "we could
not decide" into a quantitative statement of what the study was able to rule
out.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-min-rope
cf |>
  mutate(sd_units = Min_ROPE / link_sd[Response]) |>
  arrange(sd_units) |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response), Predictor = plab(Predictor),
            `min ROPE, link scale` = Min_ROPE,
            `min ROPE, SD units` = sd_units,
            `min ROPE, response scale` = sprintf("+/- %s %s",
              fmt(abs(Min_ROPE_resp), 1), Min_ROPE_unit)) |>
  kt(caption = "The smallest ROPE this design could have accepted, per slope, ordered from the best-resolved to the worst. Read the last column as: an effect smaller than this, in the response's own units, is what the study can rule out; an effect larger than this it cannot.", digits = 3)
```

# Sensitivity analysis {#sec-sensitivity}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.
:::

Six fits, identical in every respect except the prior, each changing **one**
element of the reference specification. A full factorial was not run: the
point is to attribute any change to a single choice.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-specs
kt(data.frame(
  Fit = c("REF", names(prior_specs)[-1]),
  `Prior change` = c(prior_specs$REF$label,
                     sapply(prior_specs[-1], function(x) x$label)),
  Rationale = c(prior_specs$REF$note, sapply(prior_specs[-1], function(x) x$note)),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL),
  caption = "The six prior specifications. REF is the reference; each of S1 to S5 changes exactly one line of it.")
```

## Broad prior {#sec-5a}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.A.
:::

**S2** widens every slope prior by a factor of 2.5, to
`normal(0, 2.5 x SD_link)`. This is the "broad prior" the guideline asks for:
if the posterior barely moves when the prior is made two and a half times
more permissive, the prior is not carrying the result. **S3** and **S4**
play the same role for the locality SD, and **S5** for the correlation
matrix.

## Item not applicable {#sec-5b}

::: {.na}
**BARG 5.B** asks for sensitivity to a *genuinely informed* prior --- one
built from previous studies of the same quantities. No such prior exists for
these seven measures in Quina assemblages: there is no published posterior or
meta-analytic estimate of, for instance, how edge angle varies with elevation
above a channel. Every prior used here is weakly informative by construction
(@sec-priors). The item is inapplicable, and its inapplicability is itself a
statement about how little is known.
:::

## Variations of the default priors {#sec-5c}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.C.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-sens-icc
#| fig-cap: "Q1 under all six priors: the cumulative posterior distribution of each ICC. The shaded band is the ICC ROPE [0, 0.05]. A curve's height where it crosses the right edge of the band is P(ICC <= 0.05)."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("sensitivity_icc.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sens-slopes
#| fig-cap: "Q2 under all six priors, for the slopes most exposed to the prior: the three edge-angle slopes (the response that was prior-dominated under the original specification) and the height slope of every response. Cumulative distributions on the standardised axis, with the ROPE shaded."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("sensitivity_slopes.png"))
```

Cumulative distributions rather than densities, because this report's
summaries are quantiles: a horizontal slice at 0.025 and 0.975 reads off the
interval limits directly, and the vertical distance between two curves at the
ROPE edge is the change in the quantity the decision rule uses.

BARG asks for the numbers as well as the pictures, for every parameter and
not only the plotted ones:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-full
#| tbl-cap: "Posterior median and 95% equal-tailed interval for every ICC and every slope, under each of the six priors. Slopes are standardised by the link-scale SD of their response."
sens_long |>
  mutate(cell = ci(Median, lo, hi, 2)) |>
  select(Quantity, Spec, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Spec, values_from = cell) |>
  kt(caption = NULL)
```

## Item not applicable {#sec-5d}

::: {.na}
**BARG 5.D** asks for the sensitivity of the Bayes factor to the prior. No
Bayes factor is computed (@sec-goals). Inapplicable. This is worth one extra
sentence rather than a bare dismissal: BF sensitivity is singled out in the
guideline precisely because Bayes factors are notoriously prior-dependent in
a way posterior estimates are not, which is part of why this analysis is
framed as estimation.
:::

## Do the conclusions change? {#sec-5e}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.E. The criterion is not whether the numbers moved --- they
always move --- but whether they moved enough, relative to the width of the
posterior interval and relative to the ROPE, to change a conclusion.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-verdict
sens_verdict <- sens_long |>
  mutate(is_icc = startsWith(Quantity, "ICC: "),
         Decision = ifelse(is_icc,
           ifelse(lo > ICC_ROPE, "locality variation present",
             ifelse(hi < ICC_ROPE, "negligible", "undecided")),
           rope_verdict(lo, hi, 100 * inrope, ROPE_SD))) |>
  select(Quantity, Spec, Decision) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Spec, values_from = Decision)
changed <- sens_verdict |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(n_distinct_dec = n_distinct(c_across(all_of(names(SENS))))) |>
  ungroup()
kt(changed |> select(-n_distinct_dec),
   caption = "The decision each quantity receives under each prior.")
```

```{r}
#| label: sens-readout
#| echo: false
n_changed <- sum(changed$n_distinct_dec > 1)
worst_shift <- sens_long |>
  group_by(Quantity) |>
  summarise(shift = max(Median) - min(Median),
            width = mean(hi - lo), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(rel = shift / width) |> arrange(desc(rel))
```

Of the `r nrow(changed)` quantities, **`r n_changed`**
`r if (n_changed == 1) "receives" else "receive"` a different
decision under at least one of the six priors`r if (n_changed > 0) paste0(": ", paste(changed$Quantity[changed$n_distinct_dec > 1], collapse = "; ")) else ""`.
`r if (n_changed > 0) "Those rows are the ones a reader should treat as prior-dependent; the rest are not." else "No conclusion in this report turns on the choice among the six priors."`
The largest movement of a
posterior median across the six priors, relative to the average width of that
quantity's own 95% interval, is
**`r fmt(worst_shift$rel[1] * 100, 1)`%** of the interval width, for
`r worst_shift$Quantity[1]`; for
`r sum(worst_shift$rel < 0.1)` of the `r nrow(worst_shift)` quantities the
movement is under a tenth of the interval width.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-shift
worst_shift |>
  transmute(Quantity,
            `range of medians` = shift,
            `mean interval width` = width,
            `shift as a share of the width` = rel) |>
  head(15) |>
  kt(caption = "The fifteen quantities whose posterior median moves most across the six priors, as a fraction of their own interval width.", digits = 3)
```

---

# Interpretation {#sec-interpretation}

## Q1: is there technological variation between localities? {#sec-q1}

```{r}
#| label: q1-readout
#| echo: false
icc_dec <- icc_ref |> arrange(desc(Median))
present <- icc_dec |> filter(Verdict == "locality variation present")
undec   <- icc_dec |> filter(Verdict == "undecided")
icc_j <- icc_ref |> select(Response, ref = Median, ref_lo = CrI_lo) |>
  left_join(icc_nol |> select(Response, nol = Median), by = "Response") |>
  mutate(change = ref - nol, rel = change / nol)   # positive = ICC rose

# how the Q1 decision behaves across the six priors
icc_sens <- sens_long |>
  filter(startsWith(Quantity, "ICC: ")) |>
  mutate(Resp = sub("^ICC: ", "", Quantity),
         dec = ifelse(lo > ICC_ROPE, "present",
               ifelse(hi < ICC_ROPE, "negligible", "undecided")))
icc_stable <- icc_sens |> group_by(Resp) |>
  summarise(k = n_distinct(dec), ref = dec[Spec == "REF"], .groups = "drop")
firm  <- icc_stable |> filter(k == 1, ref == "present")
flips <- icc_stable |> filter(k > 1)
flip_detail <- icc_sens |> semi_join(flips, by = "Resp") |> filter(dec != "present")
```

**Yes, for `r nrow(present)` of the seven measures under the reference prior,
and for `r nrow(firm)` of them under every prior tried.**

`r nrow(present)` responses --- `r paste(rlab(present$Response), collapse = ", ")`
--- have a 95% interval for the locality share of link-scale variance that
lies entirely above 0.05, so the null value of a negligible locality effect is
rejected under the rule of @sec-decision-rule. Their posterior medians are
`r paste(fmt(present$Median, 2), collapse = ", ")`, meaning that between
`r fmt(min(present$Median) * 100, 0)`% and `r fmt(max(present$Median) * 100, 0)`%
of the link-scale variance in those measures sits between localities rather
than within them. The remaining `r nrow(undec)` are undecided: their intervals
run from near zero to values that would be substantial, and the design does
not separate the two.

This is the only part of the analysis that returns a decisive answer, so it is
worth being precise about how far it survives the prior (@tbl-sens-verdict).

`r if (nrow(firm) > 0) sprintf("For %s the decision is 'locality variation present' under every one of the six priors.", paste(firm$Resp, collapse = " and ")) else ""`
`r if (nrow(flips) > 0) sprintf("For %s it is not: the 2.5%% limit sits so close to the 0.05 bound that %s pushes it just below, and the verdict becomes undecided (2.5%% limit %s under %s, against %s under the reference). The median barely moves -- %s against %s -- so this is a decision flipping on a boundary, not an estimate changing.", paste(unique(flip_detail$Resp), collapse = " and "), paste(unique(flip_detail$Spec), collapse = " and "), fmt(flip_detail$lo[1], 3), flip_detail$Spec[1], fmt(icc_sens$lo[icc_sens$Resp == flip_detail$Resp[1] & icc_sens$Spec == "REF"], 3), fmt(flip_detail$Median[1], 3), fmt(icc_sens$Median[icc_sens$Resp == flip_detail$Resp[1] & icc_sens$Spec == "REF"], 3)) else "No ICC decision changes under any of the six priors."`

The safe reading is therefore the stronger and narrower one: **`r nrow(firm)`
of the seven measures carry between-locality variation that no prior in the
sensitivity set can explain away**`r if (nrow(flips) > 0) sprintf(", and %s sits on the boundary", paste(unique(flip_detail$Resp), collapse = " and ")) else ""`.

**The direct test that the landscape terms are not what is producing it.** A
second model was fitted with the landscape terms removed entirely, leaving
`~ 1 + (1 |p| Locality)`. If basin, elevation and distance were carrying the
between-locality signal, dropping them would inflate the locality variance
component; equivalently, adding them to the intercept-only model would deflate
it. The comparison sidesteps the wide intervals on the individual slopes
altogether.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-icc-compare
icc_ref |> select(Response, m_ref = Median, lo_ref = CrI_lo, hi_ref = CrI_hi) |>
  left_join(icc_nol |> select(Response, m_nol = Median, lo_nol = CrI_lo, hi_nol = CrI_hi),
            by = "Response") |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response),
            `intercept only` = ci(m_nol, lo_nol, hi_nol, 3),
            `with landscape terms` = ci(m_ref, lo_ref, hi_ref, 3),
            `change in the median` = m_ref - m_nol,
            `as a share of the intercept-only median` = (m_ref - m_nol) / m_nol) |>
  kt(caption = "The ICC with and without the three landscape terms. A large negative change would mean the landscape terms had absorbed between-locality variance; a change near zero means they explain almost none of it.", digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: q1-readout2
#| echo: false
med_rel <- median(icc_j$rel)
n_up    <- sum(icc_j$change > 0); n_dn <- sum(icc_j$change < 0)
worst_j <- icc_j |> arrange(rel) |> slice(1)
best_j  <- icc_j |> arrange(desc(rel)) |> slice(1)
```

**The three landscape terms do not absorb any of the between-locality
variance.** If they explained it, the locality share would fall when they
enter the model. It does not fall: the median change across the seven
responses is `r sprintf("%+.1f", med_rel * 100)`% of the intercept-only
value, `r n_up` of the seven go up and `r n_dn` go down, and the individual
changes run from `r sprintf("%+.0f", worst_j$rel * 100)`%
(`r rlab(worst_j$Response)`) to
`r sprintf("%+.0f", best_j$rel * 100)`% (`r rlab(best_j$Response)`) --- the
largest of which starts from an intercept-only median of only
`r fmt(best_j$nol, 3)`, so the ratio is unstable rather than meaningful.
That pattern is noise about zero, not explanation. It is direct evidence on
Q2 and it does not depend on any single coefficient being well resolved:
whatever separates the localities, these three landscape variables are not
carrying it.

## Q2: do the landscape variables explain it? {#sec-q2}

```{r}
#| label: q2-readout
#| echo: false
v_tab <- table(cf$Verdict)
n_und <- sum(cf$Verdict == "undecided")
n_rej <- sum(cf$Verdict == "reject the null value")
n_acc <- sum(cf$Verdict == "accept the null value")
best  <- cf |> arrange(Min_ROPE / link_sd[Response]) |> head(3)
worst2 <- cf |> arrange(desc(Min_ROPE / link_sd[Response])) |> head(3)
dir_max <- cf |> arrange(desc(Dir_certainty)) |> head(3)
# the edge-angle ICC across the six priors, quoted in the limitations below
ea     <- sens_long |> filter(Quantity == paste0("ICC: ", rlab("EdgeAngle")))
ea_ref <- ea |> filter(Spec == "REF")
ea_min <- ea |> arrange(Median) |> slice(1)
```

**No landscape variable is shown to matter, and for most of them the study
also cannot show that they do not.**

Of the `r nrow(cf)` slopes, at the 0.1 SD ROPE:
`r n_rej` reject the null value, `r n_acc` accept it, and **`r n_und` are
undecided**. The intervals are simply too wide for the ROPE: with
`r n_loc` localities carrying every predictor, and a single binary contrast
standing in for "basin", that is what the design can deliver.

```{r}
#| label: q2-accepted
#| echo: false
acc <- cf |> filter(Verdict == "accept the null value")
```

`r if (n_acc > 0) sprintf("What the analysis can state positively is confined to %s: %s.", if (n_acc == 1) "a single slope" else sprintf("%d slopes", n_acc), paste(sprintf("%s with %s (%s on the standardised axis, %s%% of the posterior inside the ROPE)", rlab(acc$Response), tolower(plab(acc$Predictor)), ci(acc$Std_median, acc$Std_lo, acc$Std_hi, 2), fmt(acc$pct_in_ROPE, 1)), collapse = "; ")) else "No slope can be positively called practically zero at this bound either."`

Direction certainty tells the same story from the other side. The largest
value over all `r nrow(cf)` slopes is
`r fmt(max(cf$Dir_certainty), 3)`
(`r rlab(dir_max$Response[1])` ~ `r plab(dir_max$Predictor[1])`); a value of
0.5 would mean the posterior is split evenly about zero. Nothing here
approaches the near-certainty of sign that would be needed to claim a
directional landscape effect.

The one place a reader should not over-read the "undecided" label is the set
of slopes with a *small* minimum acceptable ROPE (@tbl-min-rope). For the
three best-resolved slopes the 95% interval is contained within
`r fmt(max(best$Min_ROPE / link_sd[best$Response]), 2)` SD, so while the
analysis will not call them zero at a tenth of an SD, it does rule out
anything larger than the following:
`r paste(sprintf("%s with %s, +/- %s %s", rlab(best$Response), tolower(plab(best$Predictor)), fmt(abs(best$Min_ROPE_resp), 0), best$Min_ROPE_unit), collapse = "; ")`.
That is a real, if modest, constraint. At the other extreme,
`r paste(sprintf("%s ~ %s", rlab(worst2$Response), plab(worst2$Predictor)), collapse = "; ")`
are effectively uninformative: their intervals span
`r fmt(max(worst2$Min_ROPE / link_sd[worst2$Response]), 1)` SD or more, and no
bound a reader would accept as negligible lies inside them.

## What this study can and cannot resolve {#sec-resolution-limits}

1. **The effective sample size for Q2 is `r n_loc`, not `r n_spec`.** All
   three predictors are locality attributes. The specimen count buys precision
   on the within-locality spread and on the locality offsets, not on the
   landscape slopes.

2. **The basin contrast is one comparison of
   `r sum(tapply(as.character(mod_dat$Basin), mod_dat$Locality, function(x) x[1]) == "Binchuan")`
   localities against
   `r sum(tapply(as.character(mod_dat$Basin), mod_dat$Locality, function(x) x[1]) == "Huangping")`.**
   Its interval will not narrow by collecting more specimens from the same
   localities.

3. **The assemblages are extremely unequal.** One locality supplies
   `r max(table(mod_dat$Locality))` of the `r n_spec` specimens and
   `r sum(table(mod_dat$Locality) == 1)` supply one each. Partial pooling
   handles this correctly but cannot manufacture information.

4. **The 21 correlations are weakly identified.** Estimating a 7 x 7
   correlation matrix from `r n_loc` clusters is asking a great deal;
   @tbl-cor should be read as a description of the fitted structure, not as a
   set of findings. S5 shows how much the LKJ concentration moves them.

5. **The `sd` priors carry the same scale defect the slope priors were fixed
   for, and it is visible in the results.** The reference `student_t(3, 0, 2)`
   on the locality SD is *not* rescaled per response, unlike the slope prior
   (@sec-priors). For edge angle, measured in degrees with a link-scale SD of
   `r fmt(link_sd[["EdgeAngle"]], 1)`, a prior with scale 2 is restrictive;
   for log thickness, whose link-scale SD is
   `r fmt(link_sd[["Thickness"]], 2)`, it is extremely loose. The sensitivity
   analysis shows this is not hypothetical: the edge-angle ICC is
   `r ci(ea_ref$Median, ea_ref$lo, ea_ref$hi, 3)` under the reference prior
   and `r ci(ea_min$Median, ea_min$lo, ea_min$hi, 3)` under `r ea_min$Spec`,
   the largest prior-driven movement of any ICC in the set --- and it happens
   to the response whose measurement scale is furthest from the prior's.
   `r ea_min$Spec` replaces the heavy-tailed half-$t$ with a prior whose tail
   dies quickly, and on a scale measured in degrees that is a strong
   statement. The right fix is the one already applied to the slopes: scale
   the locality SD prior to each response's own link-scale SD. That
   specification was not among the six that the one-at-a-time design called
   for here, and it is the clearest open refinement of this model. Until it is
   made, the edge-angle ICC should be read as prior-sensitive. The measures
   that carry the Q1 answer are far less exposed: their link-scale SDs are
   small enough that `student_t(3, 0, 2)` is uninformative for them, and
   `r paste(firm$Resp, collapse = " and ")` hold their decision under all six
   priors`r if (nrow(flips) > 0) sprintf(" while %s changes only because its 2.5%% limit is already touching the bound", paste(unique(flip_detail$Resp), collapse = " and ")) else ""`.

6. **Retouch generations are discrete and modelled as continuous** (@sec-post-pred),
   and **GMsize contains Thickness** (@sec-data) while the model assumes
   independent residuals across responses.

---

# Reproducibility {#sec-reproducibility}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 6.
:::

## Install the software

```
R                4.5.2 or later
CmdStan          2.39.0     (install with cmdstanr::install_cmdstan())
R packages       brms, cmdstanr, posterior, bayesplot, here, readxl,
                 dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, patchwork, knitr, quarto (CLI)
```

The backend must be **cmdstanr**. An rstan fit of the same model with the same
seed is a valid fit but not the same fit, and the CmdStan version above is
part of the specification: `sessionInfo()` records the R packages and not the
C++ toolchain that actually produced the draws.

## Retrieve the files

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `data/Quina_scraper_surface.xlsx` | specimen measurements, sheet "Quina scraper" |
| `data/Site_information.xlsx` | locality attributes: basin, height above channel, distance to channel |
| `paper/barg/barg_data.R` | builds the analysis frame; defines `link_sd`, the ROPE unit |
| `paper/barg/barg_priors.R` | all six prior specifications, in full |
| `paper/barg/barg_fits.R` | runs and caches the nine MCMC fits |
| `paper/barg/barg_quantities.R` | every derived quantity: ICC, ROPE curves, HDI, MCSE, decisions |
| `paper/barg/barg_theme.R` | the figure style, copied from the manuscript pipeline |
| `paper/barg/barg_figures.R` | every figure |
| `paper/barg/barg_dummy_data.R` | the synthetic dataset described below |
| `paper/barg/barg_report.qmd` | this document |
| `paper/barg/fits/*.rds` | the cached fits, one per specification, written with `saveRDS()` |
| `paper/barg/figures/*.png` | every figure at 300 dpi |

`paper/_analysis.R` fits the same model for the two summary tables of the
supplementary information, leaving the slope prior at `normal(0, 1)` --- which
is specification S1 of @sec-sensitivity. It is not used by any of the files
above and is not modified by them.

**Archive DOI:** `<10.17605/OSF.IO/XXXXXX>` --- to be minted on OSF or Zenodo
at submission. The deposit will contain the four source files above, the
`paper/barg/` scripts, the cached fits, and the rendered HTML.

**If the specimen data cannot be released**, `paper/barg/barg_dummy_data.R`
generates a synthetic dataset with the same columns, types, ranges, locality
structure and missingness pattern as the real one, so that a reader can verify
that the scripts run end to end without access to the measurements. It is
simulated from the fitted model and reproduces no individual specimen.

## Run the analysis

```bash
Rscript paper/barg/barg_fits.R        # nine MCMC runs; caches to paper/barg/fits/
Rscript paper/barg/barg_figures.R     # reads the cache, writes paper/barg/figures/
quarto render paper/barg/barg_report.qmd
```

The first step is the only expensive one. `barg_fits.R` writes one `.rds` per
specification and reads it back on any later run, so the second and third
steps never resample, and re-rendering this document does not re-fit anything.
To force a refit, delete the file in question. `BARG_QUICK=1` runs the whole
pipeline at reduced iterations into `paper/barg/fits_quick/`, for testing the
plumbing without disturbing the cache.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fit-times
kt(data.frame(Fit = names(mf$minutes),
              `Wall-clock minutes` = round(unname(mf$minutes), 1),
              check.names = FALSE),
   caption = "Time taken by each run on the machine that produced this document. NA means the fit was read from cache on this run.", digits = 1)
```

## Session information

```{r}
#| label: session
#| attr-output: "style='max-height:420px;overflow:auto;'"
cat("CmdStan version:", mf$cmdstan, "\n")
cat("Fits produced at:", format(mf$fitted_at, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z"), "\n\n")
sessionInfo()
```
